turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Nice to meet you too, doc. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just always feel like I’ve got this motor humming under my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like during the morning staff meetings at the building I clean, or those long church event briefings. 

Actually, the church just got these new pews installed last month. They look real nice, solid oak I think, but they are incredibly stiff. The old ones had these red cushions that were starting to tear—I know because I'm the one who always ended up sweeping the little yellow foam crumbs off the floor after service. I don't mind the sweeping, it keeps me busy, you know? I like being on my feet, getting things done. 

But sitting in those new pews... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, if I have to sit in a meeting or a briefing, I just end up shifting around the whole time, or standing up in the back, or I'll just find some excuse to go check the trash cans or move around. I just can't stay put.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient gets distracted by a tangential thought about church pews and loses their train of thought during the response.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient states they end up 'shifting around the whole time' when they have to sit in a meeting.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient admits to standing up in the back or finding excuses to move around during meetings where they are expected to remain seated.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes feeling a 'motor humming under my skin' whenever they are supposed to sit still, indicating internal restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes feeling like they have a 'motor humming' inside them and prefers being on their feet and constantly busy.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually energetic or wired for days at a time?
turns.patient_response:
Wired for days? No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm always kind of on the go, like I said, but not like... not a special period where I'm buzzing more than usual. 

The only time I was really up and running for days straight was when we had that massive pipe burst on the third floor at work. Oh man, what a disaster. Water was just pouring down into the accounting department. I told the building manager—Frank, his name is—I told him, "Frank, those pipes have been rattling for weeks." But nobody listens to the cleaning guy until the ceiling tiles cave in, right? It soaked right through the drywall. I actually had to drive over and rent three extra wet vacs from the hardware store down the street. The kid working the rental counter couldn't figure out his own barcode scanner... took him forever. I was practically bouncing on my heels waiting for him to print the receipt. 

But, uh, anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, being wired. No, I don't get like that. It's just my regular everyday energy, really.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes 'bouncing on my heels' while waiting, which indicates fidgeting with their feet.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states they are 'always kind of on the go' with a high level of 'regular everyday energy.'
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient demonstrates impatience and difficulty waiting, noting they were bouncing on their heels while waiting for the clerk to finish printing a receipt.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies experiencing distinct periods of being unusually energetic or 'wired for days at a time.'

turns.doctor_question: Do you often lose track of what you were saying or doing, even when you're trying to pay attention?
turns.patient_response:
Lose track? No, not really. I mean, I usually know exactly what I'm doing. Like, if I'm stripping and waxing the floors in the main lobby, you can't lose track of a job like that, or you'll leave streaks everywhere. We use this industrial-grade wax now, comes in these massive five-gallon buckets. Heavy as all get out. My buddy Lou—he used to work with me before he retired and moved down to Florida. Somewhere near Tampa, I think? Or maybe Sarasota. He sent me a postcard of a pelican once, standing on a pier. Anyway, Lou used to say if you don't use the right buffing pad, the floor ends up looking like a cloudy mirror. He was a real stickler for the buffer machine. We had this old Clarke floor buffer that would pull to the left if you weren't holding it tight... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Did you mean losing track of what I'm doing, or what I'm saying? Because, well, I guess I do kind of lose my train of thought when I'm talking sometimes, like just now. But with my actual work and my tasks? No, I never lose track of that. I'm pretty on top of it, I just like to keep moving.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient admits to losing their train of thought while talking, which they demonstrate by going on a tangent.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly states that they 'just like to keep moving.'
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient provides a long, rambling, tangential story about floor waxing and a former coworker before returning to the question.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies losing track of their actual work and tasks, stating they are 'pretty on top of it.'

turns.doctor_question: When you were a child, were you already the kind of person who had trouble sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, oh yeah. Even back then. I remember in grade school, I was always getting into trouble for popping out of my seat. I'd be talking over the teacher, or I'd just rush ahead and start doing the assignment before they even finished giving the directions. My mother, she used to say I acted like I was wound too tight, even when I was little. 

She used to buy these little wind-up tin toys from the five-and-dime downtown. You don't see those anymore. Everything is plastic and takes batteries now. But these were real tin, painted bright colors. She had this one that was a little drummer boy, and you'd turn the key on his back until it wouldn't turn anymore, and then you'd set him down and he'd just go crazy on that little drum. Thwack-thwack-thwack-thwack! He'd vibrate right off the edge of the kitchen table if you didn't catch him. The table had this yellow Formica top with a metal rim... my dad hated that table because the metal rim would catch on his shirt sleeves. 

But yeah, my mom would point at that little drummer boy and say, "That's you, always wound up as tight as you can go." So, yeah, I guess I've always been this way.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states getting into trouble in grade school for 'popping out of my seat'.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient describes acting like they were 'wound too tight' and compares their childhood behavior to a wind-up toy going crazy, which aligns with acting as if driven by a motor.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions 'talking over the teacher', indicating interrupting or intruding on others.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often blurt things out or interrupt people before they’ve finished talking?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I guess I do that a fair bit. Like, when my supervisor is talking, or one of the staff over at the church where I help out. If they start giving me instructions for a job, I just... I jump right in with what I think they’re going to say before they even finish. I just want to get moving, you know? But then half the time I get it wrong and they have to stop and correct me. 

Speaking of the church, though, you should see the boiler they have down in the basement. It’s this massive, ancient cast-iron thing. Takes up half the room. The guy who used to maintain it—Mr. Henderson—he just passed away last spring. Great guy. He always wore these heavy-duty suspenders with little trout painted on the clips. He was a huge fisherman. He used to go up to Lake George every August with his two grandsons. They had this little aluminum rowboat with a tiny outboard motor that sounded like a lawnmower... 

Anyway, I don't know why I brought up the boat. But yeah, when people are talking, especially giving directions, I definitely cut them off. I just get ahead of them and blurt things out.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they jump in and blurt out what they think people are going to say before they finish speaking.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to frequently cutting people off when they are talking.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech by drifting into a long, unrelated story about a church boiler, a deceased maintenance man, and his fishing trips before returning to the original topic.
